chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Musa ibn Bakr from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who hired a ship from a sailor and loaded it with food, and stipulated upon him that if the food decreased, it would be upon him [the sailor]. He said, 'It is permissible.' I said, 'But perhaps the food increases.' He said, 'The sailor claims that he added something to it.' I said, 'No.' He said, 'The increase belongs to the owner of the food, and the decrease is upon him [the sailor], if he had stipulated that upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on cargo loss and surplus in a hired ship contract according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the principle of 'gharar' (uncertainty) in maritime logistics, establishing that the default presumption is that any surplus remains with the owner unless the sailor proves he added it. It highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on precise contractual stipulations to prevent disputes over cargo weight, reflecting the practical economic concerns of the early Islamic period. The ruling underscores the importance of burden of proof in commercial transactions, a key theme in Usul al-Fiqh.
